title: Pneumatology
summary: The cited passages portray the Spirit’s work in creation, renewal, teaching, witness, and life. Genesis opens with God’s Spirit over the waters; Ezekiel promises cleansing, a new heart, and God’s Spirit enabling obedience; Joel announces an outpouring across social groups. In John, Jesus promises the Advocate; Acts depicts the Spirit coming at Pentecost; Romans describes life in the Spirit and adoption. The references show a range of roles, not one interchangeable description.
historical_context: The references move from Genesis and Israel’s prophets to Jesus’ farewell teaching, the Pentecost account, and Paul’s letter to Rome. These settings are identified from the biblical texts; the source list does not provide separate historical research for a broader reconstruction.
ancient_near_east_context: Ancient background for Pneumatology includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Genesis 1:1-2, Ezekiel 36:24-28, spirit-theme, and acts without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
canonical_context: Ezekiel’s promise of a new heart and Spirit and Joel’s promise of an outpouring are followed in this selection by Jesus’ promise of the Advocate and Acts’ account at Pentecost. Romans then describes the Spirit’s role in life and adoption. The texts invite readers to notice continuity in divine action while retaining each passage’s particular emphasis.
literary_context: The set includes a creation narrative, prophetic promises, farewell teaching, a narrative of Pentecost, and an argument in Romans. Genesis depicts the Spirit at creation; Ezekiel and Joel speak in promises; John records Jesus’ teaching; Acts narrates an event; Romans explains life in the Spirit. The genre changes affect what each passage says about the Spirit.
covenantal_significance: Ezekiel connects the Spirit with cleansing, a new heart, and faithful life; Joel describes the Spirit being poured out; Acts narrates a community’s reception of the Spirit; Romans relates the Spirit to life and adoption. Read with John’s promise of the Advocate, these passages connect renewal, presence, witness, and belonging without reducing them to one function.
canonical_role: This entry traces selected biblical portrayals of the Spirit from creation through prophetic promises to Jesus’ teaching and the early church’s experience and instruction. The cited texts supply distinct pieces of that account.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Pneumatology in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
